| [NOTE-157](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-157.md) v2 | Roberts — Talkative AI and the fiction of artificial minds | If a substantial class of mental states (interoceptive, affective, perceptual, and bodily-agentive states such as effort, trying and ownership) depends on an animate body, then today's disembodied chatbots lack them, and their many self-ascriptions of such states are "systematically untrue". | [NOTE-180](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-180.md) v4 | Clark & Chalmers — The Extended Mind | The paper argues from a functionalist parity claim that a process or standing state which would count as cognitive if it happened in the head counts as cognitive when an external resource carries it, provided the resource is actively coupled to the organism here and now. | [NOTE-331](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-331.md) | Bechara, Damasio, Tranel & Damasio — Deciding advantageously before knowing the advantageous strategy | Ten controls and six ventromedial prefrontal patients play the four-deck gambling task while anticipatory skin-conductance responses (SCRs) and verbal reports are tracked. | [NOTE-332](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-332.md) | Damasio — The somatic marker hypothesis and the possible functions of the prefrontal cortex | The somatic marker hypothesis as its author stated it in 1996. The evidence is summarised from earlier lesion and skin-conductance studies, without numbers. | [NOTE-351](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-351.md) | Intelligence without representation | A methodological manifesto with working robots behind it. | [NOTE-368](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-368.md) | Adams & Aizawa — The bounds of cognition | Adams and Aizawa grant [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md)'s parity sentence but deny that any actual case meets it. | [NOTE-467](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-467.md) | The Haken–Kelso–Bunz (HKB) model: from matter to movement to mind | Kelso's retrospective on HKB. | [NOTE-727](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-727.md) | Rubin, Roli, Stano & Damiano — Genealogies of organizational closure | A conceptual genealogy of the notions of closure (closure to information, cyclic, operational, semantic, catalytic, metabolic, closure to efficient causation, closure of constraints) from mathematical logic, cybernetics, systems theory, thermodynamics, relational biology and the biology of cognition. | [NOTE-826](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-826.md) | Turvey — Preliminaries to a theory of action | An essay, not a study. The executive cannot command muscles one by one, so acts are built from relatively autonomous coordinative structures, reflexes and their functional combinations, a term Turvey takes from Easton (1972). | [NOTE-867](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-867.md) | Hutchins — How a cockpit remembers its speeds | In an MD-80 approach, the correspondence between airspeeds and wing configurations for the day's landing weight is computed once, 25 to 30 minutes before landing, by selecting a printed speed card with the displayed gross weight, and is stored in the positions of movable bugs on both airspeed indicators; when the plane slows 10 to 15 minutes later, the needle's approach to a bug cues each flap call by a judgment of spatial proximity. Hutchins argues that this memory belongs to the cockpit as a functional system and that speed bugs do not improve any pilot's memory but replace a recall-and-scale-reading task with a perceptual one. The account is a stylized description of mandated procedure, informed by more than 100 observer flights and simulator recordings, with no measured performance, no comparison of crews with and without bugs, and no failure cases; the claim that the arrangement changes what the system can do is established by analysis of the tasks, not by data. | Read |
| [NOTE-871](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-871.md) | Kirsh — The intelligent use of space | A classification, from video of cooks, assemblers and baggers, informal observation and the Tetris studies, of how people arrange things around them to cut the time and memory a task needs: arrangements that simplify choice (hide or highlight affordances, eliminate decisions, offload heuristic properties), arrangements that simplify perception (clustering, regions, marking, the vernier effect), and spatial dynamics that save internal computation (Tetris rotation, self-cueing). | [NOTE-872](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-872.md) | Kirsh — Adapting the environment instead of oneself | A conceptual paper. It models a task as a directed graph of states and actions with a cost metric on transitions, and classifies how an agent can improve its payoff by actions external to the task: pruning hard initial states, routine maintenance, scouting ahead, tools (which change the graph), and actions that make a space more "cognitively congenial" (which leave the graph intact and reduce mental operations). It names amortization once, as a parenthetical gloss on chimps leaving nut-cracking stones in place, and gives an investment rule for maintenance (future benefit against present cost times an "interest factor" for risk) in words only. There is no cost model with reuse frequency, retrieval cost or staleness; mental cost lies outside the graph, and the paper says there is "no general theory" of congeniality. The empirical figures are unpublished pilot results. | Read |
| [NOTE-878](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-878.md) | Kirsh & Maglio — On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action | Kirsh and Maglio define an epistemic action as a physical action whose primary function is to reduce the space, time or unreliability of the agent's own mental computation, and argue from Tetris keystroke data that players rotate and translate pieces for that reason: zoids are rotated more than plan-then-act would need, rotation starts within a few hundred milliseconds of a zoid appearing, and a translate-to-wall check is used more the higher the drop. The computational saving is argued, not measured: physical rotation of 90° takes as little as 100 ms against an estimated 800–1200 ms mentally (a three-player pilot), and fewer attentional probes and less working memory are needed. The trade is physical action in place of internal computation at the moment of use, not precomputation or caching; the paper explicitly sets it against caching and chunking accounts of skill, and mentions amortized complexity only in passing for everyday cases such as sorting bolts before assembly. It says the choice fits a Stigler-style cost–benefit model in outline but that such models fail in detail, because an epistemic action's value depends on the particular internal computation it serves. | Read |
| [NOTE-883](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-883.md) | Ballard, Hayhoe, Pook & Rao — Deictic codes for the embodiment of cognition | At about a third of a second, the time scale of a saccade, the article models fixation as a pointer that binds a variable in a behavioural program to a place in the world, so that what is bound is only the task-relevant feature, fetched just before use. The authors read this as working memory having a "carrying cost" that exceeds the cost of re-acquiring from the world, but that cost is inferred from the choices and never measured or modelled, and the evidence is one task with small samples (seven subjects for the main data, three for the colour-change experiment) and no statistics reported in the article. What is left in the world is unprocessed input, not a computed result, and the article argues against precomputation where the needed products cannot be foreseen. | Read |
| [NOTE-887](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-887.md) | Risko & Gilbert — Cognitive offloading | A short review that defines cognitive offloading as physical action that changes a task's information-processing requirements to reduce cognitive demand, splits it into offloading onto the body and into the world, and proposes a metacognitive model: whether people offload is a strategy choice driven by their evaluation of internal versus extended strategies, which tracks objective internal demand but can be wrong, and offloading in turn changes both memory and those evaluations. The evidence is a handful of choice/no-choice studies, summarised qualitatively; the review reports no effect sizes and no formal account of costs. It names costs (memory for offloaded content, GPS-impaired spatial memory, photo-taking impairment, automation complacency and bias, skill decay, inflated self-knowledge, a self-reinforcing drift toward external reliance). It does not frame offloading as computation reused over time, and says nothing about how often an offloaded result is used. | Read |
| [NOTE-960](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-960.md) | Friston et al. — action and behavior: a free-energy formulation | Existence is taken to require a low-entropy ensemble density; an ergodic assumption turns that entropy into time-averaged surprise, and because the setup stipulates that action is the only way an agent changes the hidden states it senses, action as well as perception must minimize a free-energy bound on surprise. | [NOTE-1065](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1065.md) | Ward — What is enactivism? | A conceptual paper. The usual taxonomy, which lumps every view stressing sensorimotor loops as "enactivism" and splits it into autopoietic, sensorimotor and radical variants, hides what is distinctive about The Embodied Mind. A second axis, organicist against informationalist, runs across the cognitivist–embodied one. Enactivism is organicist, and it adds the primacy of lived experience and a reciprocity in which scientific vocabularies reshape the experience they describe. Most embodied views, predictive processing among them, are informationalist. It argues for a taxonomy, not for enactivism's truth. | Read |
| [NOTE-1074](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1074.md) | Wacquant — A concise genealogy and anatomy of habitus | A short essay that takes habitus back to Aristotle's hexis and to Bourdieu's first use of it, for the misfit between dispositions and a changing world in Béarn and Algeria, and clears four misreadings: habitus is multilayered and revised in practice, not the replica of one structure; it need not be coherent; it suits crisis and change as well as reproduction; and it never generates action by itself, but only as triggered by positions in a social world. | [NOTE-1093](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1093.md) | Bigand et al. — The geometry of interpersonal synchrony in human dance | In 35 dyads of untrained dancers facing each other, shared music and visual contact were varied independently.
